source_text: Malum igitur naturale esse non potest ac per hoc nec rea ulla naturaliter creatura nec malus auctor. Malum quippe non exstantis invenitur naturae, sed sicut omnis creatura, in quantum conditur, bona est, ita et Deus, naturarum auctor bonarum, nullo operis sui crimine maculatus per omnia bonus probatur. Totum igitur, quidquid Manichaeus attulerat, hac una catholicorum ratione subversum est.
pass_a_gloss: Evil therefore cannot be natural, and through this neither is any creature naturally defendant nor an evil author. For evil is found not of a nature existing, but as every creature, insofar as it is founded, is good, so also God, author of good natures, stained by no crime of his work is proved through all good. The whole therefore, whatever the Manichaean had brought, has been subverted by this one reason of catholics.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Evil, then, cannot be natural. Consequently, no creature is guilty by nature, nor is its author evil. For evil is found not to be a subsisting nature. Just as every creature is good insofar as it is created, so God, the author of good natures, is proved entirely good, stained by no crime in his work. Everything Mani brought forward is therefore overthrown by this single catholic argument (1 Timothy 4:4).

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
For Julian, sin requires rational choice; infants lack usus rationis.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Every creature is good repeats the scriptural affirmation.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
